$comment: ROADMAP Phase 1A step 7 - guard and evasion. This is where Decision 0010 stops being architecture: the ten named guards of docs/design/boxing_guard_matchups.md land as authored postures that modulate the coverage extents of the two collision volumes, and evasion lands as an active choice that outranks covering. Engine-neutral definitions only; no implementation is claimed (Rule 18). Every number is a tuning hypothesis. Semantics: docs/phase1a/guard_and_evasion.md.

authority.$comment: Rule 13. Nothing here decides whether an attack was blocked - the collision pipeline does. This file decides what shape a fighter is in when it asks.

postures.notes: The staple. Covers the head cluster well and sells the body - the trade that makes body investment pay (Rule 4 counterplay against passive blocking).
The best all-round close coverage in the set, priced in stamina - it collapses when conditioning fades, which is the intended failure mode rather than a nerf.
Highest counter readiness, lowest structural coverage. The lead hand is down: the jab is a baseline weakness that ringcraft narrows but never closes (guard doc reconciliation item 4).
High absorption, low counter speed, poor vision. Its uppercut coverage is conditional on bar alignment - reconciliation item 1, mechanized by Decision 0010.
Distance control. The overhand looping over the extended arm is its signature vulnerability - not something it smothers (guard doc, ruled).
Nothing here is structurally protected; the value is vision and baiting. The structure that ages worst as reflex attributes decay.
The mirror of the high guard, and the correct intercept structure for chin-target uppercuts because it bars the rising path.
A survival posture, not a platform. Maximum head coverage bought with the body, the ring, vision and all offense - it must never be an indefinitely safe state (Rule 4).
An inside control tool rather than a pure block: it disrupts entry paths and buys exit angles.
Strong against predictable singles, beaten by feints and layered volume - too many threats to parry at once.

evasions.notes: Vacates the head lane without ceding range - the cheapest way to make a straight punch pay whiff cost.
Lowers level under an arc; the uppercut is the punishment because it rises into where the head is going.
Range denial rather than evasion: it removes the fighter from reach instead of vacating a lane, and scores nothing. Repeated without offense it reads as empty avoidance (Rule 21 Long Drain).
Changes the angle rather than the distance; the primary corner escape and the reason ring cutting is a skill.

evasion_economy.$comment: Rule 13 tier order made operational. The collision pipeline already ranks active_evasion above guard_intercept; this is why that ordering is correct rather than arbitrary.
evasion_economy.notes: A committed evasion that misses its window leaves the defender in recovery with no structure up - the price of choosing the active answer. Slipping is better than blocking when it works and worse when it does not, which is what makes it a decision.

guard_integrity.$comment: Rule 14. Blocking reduces clean damage without erasing consequence, and the erosion must come from intelligent varied pressure rather than from repetition alone (Rule 4).
guard_integrity.opened_state: posture drops to its weaker alignment state until restored
guard_integrity.notes: A broken guard is not a stun: it moves the posture to its weak alignment state, which the collision model reads as reduced coverage extents. Nothing is disabled and no input is eaten.

prohibitions: Resolve contact in this file; the collision pipeline is the sole authority (Rule 13).
Branch any behaviour on a posture's identity rather than on the coverage extents it produces (Decision 0010).
Grant a posture that covers every lane, or one that covers none - every guard is a trade.
Open a guard through predictable single-action spam rather than intelligent varied pressure (Rule 14).
Let a survival posture remain indefinitely safe or freely offensive (Rule 4).
Rank passive covering above active evasion in reward (Rule 13).

invariants.statement: No posture covers both volumes at full extent, and none covers neither; every posture sells one lane to buy another.
Every posture extent names a declared guard volume and sits inside that volume's modulation range in the collision model.

Every posture declares at least one alignment state, and the two postures whose conditional coverage canon reconciles - cross-arm and Philly shell - declare exactly the state ids the collision model's worked examples use.
A posture with no cheap offense must pay for it in mobility, vision or stamina; maximum coverage is never free.
Active evasion is rewarded above passive covering and carries a real mistime penalty, matching the collision pipeline's stage order and the punch model's recovery differential.

Every evasion maps to a move-table entry; active-window evasions carry active_ticks equal to the move table exactly and vacate at least one hurtbox-backed region, while positional answers vacate nothing because they remove the fighter from reach rather than clearing a lane.
Guard integrity degrades from absorbed force and varied pressure, never from repetition count alone, and an opened guard reduces coverage rather than disabling the fighter.
This file resolves no contact and the pipeline never reads a posture identity.
